title: The Sounds That Are Hard
overview: You can already read. This unit is not the alphabet. It covers six things about English sound that learners most often find difficult — and it starts by finding out which of the six are difficult for you. Not all six will be. Which ones they are depends on the language you already speak, and that is different for everybody, so nobody can tell you the answer. You test yourself, in Practice 1, and then you spend your time on the ones that came back wrong.
learningPath: Do Practice 1 first. It takes ten minutes and tells you which of the six sounds to work on.
Read and listen to the Lesson. It explains all six.
Open Patterns. Study the cards for the sounds you got wrong, and skim the rest.
Learn the words. Each group is built around one of the six sounds.
Read the three texts aloud, not silently. One of them is a form you will meet in real life.
Record yourself, play it back, and compare it with the model. Your own recording is the correction.
Take the quiz. Every answer is explained, whether you got it right or not.
lectureScript:
Welcome. Before anything else, I want to say what this unit is not.
It is not the alphabet. You can read. You know what letters are and you know how to learn a script. Nobody here needs to be taught that A comes before B.
What this unit is about is six things. Six parts of English sound that learners find hard. And here is the important part: not all six will be hard for you.
Which ones are hard depends on the language you already speak. Every language uses a different set of sounds. English asks you to make some sounds your language may never use, and to put consonants together in ways your language may not allow. If your language already has a sound, it will not trouble you at all. If it does not, that sound will take work.
So I cannot tell you which of the six are your problem. Nobody can, without hearing you. That is why Practice 1 comes first. You record yourself, you listen back, and you find out. Ten minutes, and then you know where to spend your time.
Let me take you through the six.
Number one is th. English has two of them. Listen: the, this, that — that one uses your voice. And: three, thank, month — that one is just air. For both, your tongue comes forward, between your teeth. Most languages do not do this, so it feels wrong at first. Look in a mirror. If you cannot see your tongue, it is not far enough forward.
Number two is a family of four sounds that are easy to confuse: v, f, w and b. V and f are made the same way — top teeth on bottom lip — and the only difference is voice. V buzzes; f does not. W is different again: your lips make a small circle and your teeth are not involved. And b closes both lips completely. Four sounds, and swapping any two of them changes the word. Very. Ferry. Berry. Wary.
Number three is r and l. Say red. Now say led. For r, your tongue pulls back and does not touch anything. For l, the tip of your tongue touches the roof of your mouth, just behind your teeth. Many languages have only one sound in this area, and if yours does, these two will sound identical to you at first. That is normal, and it passes.
Number four is consonant clusters, and this one catches almost everybody. English pushes consonants together with nothing between them. School. Street. Stop. Small. Many languages do not allow that at the start of a word, so your mouth helps by adding a small vowel — and what comes out is a word the listener does not recognise. It also makes you spell it wrong, because you write what you say. Say it in one piece. School.
Number five is vowel length. Sit. Seat. Live. Leave. Full. Fool. The vowel in the second word of each pair is usually longer and has a different sound quality. That difference can change the meaning completely. For example, ‘I live here’ and ‘I leave here’ express opposite ideas.
Number six is blending. This is how you read a word nobody has taught you. S — t — o — p. Stop. Say the sounds, then run them together faster until they become the word. You will use this for the rest of your life, so it is worth ten minutes now.
That is all six. Go and do Practice 1, find out which ones are yours, and then come back.

outcomes.outcome: Identify which of the six difficult sound areas need work, by recording and comparing against a model.
outcomes.evidence: Practice 1 self-check completed, with the learner's own six-row result table filled in.
outcomes.cefrDescriptor: I can hear which English sounds I get wrong when I listen to my own recording.

outcomes.outcome: Produce both th sounds with the tongue between the teeth.
outcomes.evidence: Speaking 1 recording of the five th words; Reading 1 read aloud.
outcomes.cefrDescriptor: I can say the and three with my tongue between my teeth.

outcomes.outcome: Keep /v/, /f/, /w/ and /b/ apart in speech, and hear them apart in someone else's.
outcomes.evidence: Speaking 2 recording; Practice 3 sorting; Quiz item 3.
outcomes.cefrDescriptor: I can say very, ferry and berry so they sound like three different words.

outcomes.outcome: Say a word beginning or ending with two or three consonants without inserting a vowel.
outcomes.evidence: Speaking 4 recording of school, street, stop, small; Practice 4 self-check on the playback.
outcomes.cefrDescriptor: I can say school and street in one piece, without adding a vowel.

outcomes.outcome: Hear the difference between a short and a long English vowel in a spoken pair.
outcomes.evidence: Practice 5 discrimination, eight pairs, six or more correct.
outcomes.cefrDescriptor: I can hear whether someone said sit or seat.

outcomes.outcome: Read an unfamiliar short word by blending its sounds, and read the most common words on sight.

outcomes.cefrDescriptor: I can read a short word I have never seen before by putting its sounds together.

words.meaning: The word you put before a thing when you and the listener both know which thing you mean.
practice: The form is on the table.
The bus stop is over there.
words.tutor: Say five short sentences that each start with the. Ask the tutor whether it heard the or de.

words.meaning: The word for a thing that is here, close to you.
practice: This bus goes to the centre.
I do not understand this word.
words.tutor: This uses the th that buzzes. Say it with your tongue forward and ask the tutor if it sounded like dis.

words.meaning: The number 3.
practice: The office is on the third floor.
words.tutor: Three starts with the quiet th and goes straight into r, which is hard. Say it slowly, then faster.

words.meaning: To tell someone you are glad about what they did for you.
practice: I want to thank the doctor.
She said thank you and left.
Thank you — that is very kind.
words.tutor: You will say this every day, so it is worth getting right. Say thank you five times with your tongue forward.

words.meaning: One of the twelve parts of a year.
words.example: I have been here for one month.
practice: The rent is due next month.
I work five days a month.
words.tutor: Month has th at the end, which is harder than at the start. Hold the last sound and ask the tutor if you said mont.

words.meaning: A word you put before another word to make it stronger.
words.tutor: Very, ferry and berry are three different words. Say all three and ask the tutor which one it heard first.

words.meaning: The number 5.
words.example: I work five days a week.
words.tutor: Five ends with the v sound and it is easy to lose. Hold the last sound and check it buzzes.

words.meaning: A paper with empty spaces where you write your details.
practice: Where do I sign the form?
Bring the form and your card.
I left the form at home.
words.tutor: Form starts with f — teeth on lip, no buzz. Say form, then vorm, and ask the tutor which you said.

words.meaning: The thing you do to earn money.
words.example: I go to work at seven.
practice: How do you get to work?
words.tutor: Work starts with w — round lips, no teeth. Say work, then verk, and hear the difference.

words.meaning: Better than all the others.
practice: The best time is early morning.
She is the best in the group.
words.tutor: Best, vest and west start with three different sounds. Say all three and ask the tutor to name them.

words.meaning: Correct, or the side that is not the left.
practice: The office is on your right.
words.tutor: Right and light are different words. Say both and ask the tutor which one it heard.

words.meaning: The side that is not the right.
words.example: The bank is on the left.
practice: The door on the left is open.
The keys are on the left shelf.
words.tutor: For l the tip of your tongue touches behind your top teeth. Say left five times and feel where it touches.

words.meaning: To get to know something you did not know before.
practice: You learn a little every day.
words.tutor: Learn has l at the start and r in the middle — both of this card's sounds in one word. Say it slowly.

words.meaning: A written message you send to someone, or one sign of the alphabet.
words.example: I got a letter from the office.
practice: Write your name in capital letters.
This letter is not for me.
words.tutor: Letter has an l sound, a tapped t and an r sound. Say it three times and ask the tutor if all three were clear.

words.meaning: After now, but not much after.
practice: We can talk about it later.
words.tutor: Later and radar use both sounds in different places. Say later slowly and check the l and the r are different.

words.meaning: A place where children go to learn.
practice: The school is near the market.
There is a school in this street.
words.tutor: Say school in one breath, with no vowel before the s. Ask the tutor if it heard a sound at the start.

words.meaning: A road in a town, with buildings along it.
practice: The office is in the next street.
Cross the street at the lights.
What is the name of this street?
words.tutor: Street has three consonants at the start. Say s, then st, then str, then street.

words.meaning: To finish moving, or to make something finish moving.
words.example: The bus does not stop here.
practice: Please stop — I do not understand.
The rain stopped an hour ago.
words.tutor: Stop begins with st. Say top, then stop, and listen for anything you added at the front.

words.meaning: Not big.
practice: The office is small but clean.
Give me the small one, please.
words.tutor: Small starts with sm. Say mall, then small, and check you did not add a sound before the s.

words.meaning: The one that comes after this one.
words.example: Get off at the next stop.
practice: The office is in the next street.
The next bus is at five.
words.tutor: Next ends with three consonants. Hold the end and ask the tutor if you said nex.

words.meaning: To rest with your weight on a chair.
practice: We sit and talk after work.
Do not sit on that chair.
words.tutor: Sit has a short vowel. Say sit, then seat, and ask the tutor which one it heard first.

words.meaning: A place where you can sit, such as a chair.
practice: There is no seat on the bus.
He kept a seat for me.
The seat by the window is free.
words.tutor: Seat has a long vowel. Hold it. Then say sit, short, and hear the two lengths.

words.meaning: To have your home in a place.
practice: They live next to the school.
I lived there for three years.
My family lives in another town.
words.tutor: I live here and I leave here mean opposite things. Say both to the tutor and ask what it understood.

words.meaning: To go away from a place, or to let something stay behind.
words.example: I leave the house at seven.
practice: What time does the bus leave?
Do not leave your bag here.
She left the office at five.
I will leave the form with you.
words.tutor: Leave has the long vowel. Say leave, then live, and ask the tutor which came first.

words.meaning: With no space left inside.
practice: The form is full of questions.
The room was full this morning.
words.tutor: Full is short and fool is long. Say both and check the tutor can tell them apart.

words.meaning: The word you use when you talk about yourself.
words.tutor: English always writes I as a capital letter, anywhere in the sentence. Write three sentences about yourself and check every I.

words.meaning: The word that joins a thing to what it is, or to where it is.
practice: My bag is on the seat.
words.tutor: Many languages do not need a word here, so it gets left out. Say five sentences and check is is in every one.

words.meaning: The word that shows something belongs to you.
practice: My office is near the market.
words.tutor: Say five sentences with my and check it comes before the thing, not after it.

words.meaning: The word that says you are able to do something.
practice: I can read a little English.
words.tutor: Can never changes: I can, she can, we can — never she cans. Say all three and check you added no s.

words.meaning: A word English puts at the front to make a question or a negative.
practice: Do not leave your bag here.
words.tutor: English needs do to make most questions. Say three questions with do and three without, and hear which sound wrong.

readings.title: Six Things, and Not All Six Are Yours
readings.passage:
You can read. You do not need the alphabet.
English has six things that learners find hard. Not all six will be hard for you.
The first is th. The, this, that. Three, thank, month. Your tongue comes forward, between your teeth.
The second is v, f, w and b. Very. Ferry. Berry. Wary. Four words, four sounds, one small difference each.
The third is r and l. Right and light. Red and led.
The fourth is two consonants together. School. Street. Stop. Small. Nothing between them.
The fifth is long and short. Sit and seat. Live and leave.
The sixth is putting sounds together to read a new word. S — t — o — p. Stop.
Which of the six are hard for you? It depends on the language you already speak. Every language uses a different set of sounds. If your language has a sound, English will not trouble you with it. If it does not, that one will take work.
So nobody can tell you the answer. You have to test yourself. That is Practice 1. Do it first.

readings.title: Why People Ask You to Repeat
readings.passage:
Your grammar can be correct. Your words can be right. And a person still says: sorry, pardon?
This is not because your English is bad. It is usually one small sound.
Say the word school with a small vowel in front of it, and the listener hears a word they do not know. They stop. They are not being difficult — they simply cannot find the word.
Say ferry when you mean very, and the listener hears a real word — just not the one you meant.
Say tank you for thank you, and most people understand, because there is nothing else it can be.
That is the pattern. A sound that turns your word into another real word is expensive. A sound that turns it into no word at all is worse. A sound that leaves it obvious costs you almost nothing.
So work on the ones that cost you, and do not worry about the rest.
The fix is not to speak louder. Volume was never the problem. Speak a little slower and put the sound in the right place. Nobody minds waiting. Everybody minds not understanding.

readings.title: Learning Centre — Registration Form
readings.setting: The form you fill in on your first day at a learning centre.
readings.passage:
LEARNING CENTRE — REGISTRATION FORM
Please write in CAPITAL LETTERS.

Family name: ______________________
First name: ______________________
Date of birth: ____ / ____ / ________

Street: ______________________
Town: ______________________
Phone: ______________________

Have you studied English before?   Yes / No
If yes, for how many months? ______

Which days can you come?
[ ] Monday   [ ] Tuesday   [ ] Wednesday   [ ] Thursday   [ ] Friday

Morning or evening?   [ ] Morning   [ ] Evening

readings.passageSpeech: LEARNING CENTRE — REGISTRATION FORM. Please write in capital letters. There is a line for your family name, a line for your first name, and a line for your date of birth. Then a line for your street, a line for your town, and a line for your phone number. Have you studied English before? Yes or no. If yes, for how many months? Which days can you come? Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday or Friday. Morning or evening? Do you need a place for a child? Yes or no. At the end there is a line for your signature and a line for the date. Please return this form to the office before your first class. Bring one document that shows your name and date of birth.

comprehension.q: How many difficult things does the text describe?
comprehension.why: The title and the second line both say six. The text is deliberate about this — it is six things, not twenty-six letters.

comprehension.q: Will all six be hard for you? What does the text say it depends on?
comprehension.a: No. It depends on the language you already speak.
comprehension.why: The text says this twice: every language uses a different set of sounds, so which ones give trouble is different for each learner.

comprehension.q: Why does the text say nobody can tell you which sounds are hard for you?
comprehension.a: Because it depends on the language you already speak, so you have to test yourself.
comprehension.why: This is the reason Practice 1 comes first — the diagnosis has to come from your own recording, not from someone else's guess.

comprehension.q: Where do you put your tongue for th?
comprehension.why: It is in the line about the first difficult thing.

comprehension.q: According to the text, why does a listener stop when a word has an extra vowel in it?
comprehension.a: Because they hear a word they do not know and cannot find it.
comprehension.why: The text says the listener is not being difficult — the word simply is not one they recognise.

comprehension.q: Which kind of mistake does the text say costs you the most?
comprehension.a: One that turns your word into no word at all.
comprehension.why: The text ranks three kinds: a mistake that makes another real word is expensive, one that makes no word is worse, and one that leaves the meaning obvious costs almost nothing.

comprehension.q: What does the text say the fix is — and what is it not?
comprehension.a: The fix is to speak a little slower and put the sound in the right place. It is not to speak louder.
comprehension.why: The last lines say both halves. Speaking louder is the instinct, and the text names it in order to rule it out.

comprehension.q: How must you write on this form?
comprehension.why: The instruction is on the second line, before any of the boxes.

comprehension.q: What must you bring with the form?
comprehension.a: One document that shows your name and date of birth.
comprehension.why: It is the last line of the form, and it is the thing most people miss because they stop reading at the signature.

comprehension.q: When must the form be returned?
comprehension.why: The second-to-last line says so. A form usually has a deadline, and it is rarely where you expect it.

grammar.title: Th: tongue between the teeth
grammar.explanation: English has two th sounds and many languages have neither. Both put your tongue forward, between your teeth. One uses your voice and one is just air, but getting the tongue out is most of the work.
grammar.rule:
Quiet th: three, thank, month, both
Voiced th: the, this, that, they, mother

Tongue comes forward, between the teeth.
Air passes over it.

It will feel strange. That is correct.
grammar.workedExample:
Take the word think.
1. Put the tip of your tongue lightly between your teeth.
2. Push air over it — no voice. You get the first sound.
3. Now add the rest: think.
4. Check in a mirror. On the first sound you should SEE your tongue.
If you cannot see it, you said tink, not think. Push the tongue further forward and go again.
grammar.mistake: The commonest slip is keeping the tongue behind the teeth, which turns th into t, d or s: tink for think, dis for this. Nothing is wrong with your mouth — it is doing what it has always done. A mirror fixes this faster than listening does.
grammar.tip: If you cannot see your tongue in a mirror, it is not far enough forward.
grammar.practice:
Say these with your tongue between your teeth. Mark V for the ones that use your voice and Q for the quiet ones.
1. the
2. three
3. this
4. thank
5. month
6. mother
grammar.answers: Voiced (V): 1 the, 3 this, 6 mother. Quiet (Q): 2 three, 4 thank, 5 month. Check in a mirror — you should see your tongue on all six, whichever kind it is.

grammar.title: V, F, W and B: four sounds, one small difference each
grammar.explanation: These four are made in three different places, and swapping any two changes the word. V and F use the same mouth position and differ only by voice. W uses rounded lips and no teeth. B closes both lips.
grammar.rule:
f = top teeth on bottom lip, no voice
v = top teeth on bottom lip, voice on
w = lips round, teeth not used
b = both lips closed, then opened

very — ferry — berry — wary
vest — best — west
fine — vine
grammar.workedExample:
Take very and ferry.
1. Put your top teeth on your bottom lip. Both words start here.
2. Put a finger on your throat.
3. Say very. Your throat should buzz on the first sound.
4. Say ferry. No buzz.
That buzz is the whole difference. If your finger feels the same on both, you are saying the same word twice.
grammar.mistake: V often comes out as f or b, and w as v. The words stay close enough that people usually understand, which is exactly why this one survives for years unless you work on it deliberately.
grammar.tip: Finger on throat for v and f. Mirror for w — you should see your lips make a circle.
grammar.practice:
Which sound starts each word: F, V, W or B?
1. very
2. work
3. best
4. form
5. west
6. five
grammar.answers: 1. V  2. W  3. B  4. F  5. W  6. F (and it ENDS with V — hold the last sound and feel it buzz).

grammar.title: R and L
grammar.explanation: For l, the tip of your tongue touches the roof of your mouth just behind your top teeth. For r, your tongue pulls back and touches nothing at all. Many languages use only one sound in this area, and if yours does, these two will sound identical at first.
grammar.rule:
l = tongue tip touches, just behind the teeth
r = tongue pulls back, touches nothing

right — light
red — led
rate — late
correct — collect
grammar.workedExample:
Take light and right.
1. Say light. Stop on the first sound and hold it. Feel where your tongue is: the tip is touching, just behind your top teeth.
2. Now pull your tongue back so it touches nothing, and make a sound.
3. Add the rest: right.
If your tongue touches in both words, you said light twice.
grammar.mistake: If these two sound the same to you, that is not a problem with your ear — it is that your first language may treat them as one sound. Use touch, not hearing: the tongue either touches or it does not, and you can feel that even when you cannot hear it.
grammar.tip: l touches. r does not. Decide by feel, not by sound.
grammar.practice:
Does your tongue touch behind your teeth? Mark YES or NO.
1. left
2. right
3. learn
4. read
5. letter
6. later
grammar.answers: YES (l): 1 left, 3 learn, 5 letter (twice), 6 later. NO (r): 2 right, 4 read. Number 3 and number 6 have both sounds — the tongue touches for the l and lets go for the r.

grammar.title: Two consonants together, with nothing between them
grammar.explanation: This one catches almost everybody. English pushes consonants together at the start and end of a word. Many languages do not allow that, so the mouth helps by adding a small vowel — and the word stops being recognisable. It also makes you spell it wrong, because you write what you say.
grammar.rule:
school   street   stop   small   speak
At the end too:
next   asked   helped   works

Nothing goes between the consonants.
Build it up: s … st … str … street
grammar.workedExample:
Take street.
1. Say just the s. Hold it: ssss.
2. Add the t, with nothing between: st.
3. Add the r: str.
4. Add the rest: street.
5. Now record yourself saying it and play it back.
On the playback, listen to what happens BEFORE the s. If you hear any sound there, go back to step 1.
grammar.mistake: The added vowel is almost impossible to feel and very easy to hear on a recording. This is why the playback matters: you will hear it in your own voice long before you can feel it in your mouth.
grammar.tip: Start from the s and do not stop until the vowel arrives.
grammar.practice:
Build each word up, then say it whole, then record and play back.
1. s … sc … school
2. s … st … str … street
3. s … st … stop
4. s … sm … small
5. next (hold the end)
grammar.answers: There is no key here — your recording is the answer. Play it back and mark YES or NO for each word: did you add a sound before the s, or between the consonants? Most people have at least two YES on the first attempt. If you have none, that is one of the six you do not need to work on.

grammar.title: Long and short vowels change the word
grammar.explanation: English holds some vowels longer than others, and the length changes which word it is. This is not about speaking slowly — it is that sit and seat are two different words.
grammar.rule:
short          long
sit            seat
live           leave
full           fool
it             eat
ship           sheep
grammar.workedExample:
Take live and leave.
1. Say live. The vowel is cut short — in and out quickly.
2. Say leave. Hold the vowel: leeeave.
3. Now say I live here, then I leave here.
Those two sentences mean opposite things. If a listener cannot tell them apart, hold the long one longer than feels natural. Too long is still understood; too short is a different word.
grammar.mistake: Because both words exist, a listener will not ask you to repeat — they will simply understand the wrong one. That makes this mistake quieter than the others, and more expensive.
grammar.tip: When it matters, hold it longer. A vowel that is too long is still the right word.
grammar.practice:
Say one word from each pair out loud, record it, then listen back and write down which one you hear.
1. sit — seat
2. live — leave
3. full — fool
4. it — eat
grammar.answers: Compare what you wrote with what you meant to say. If they match on all four, this is not one of your problem areas. If they do not match, exaggerate the long vowel until they do, then bring it back down slowly.

grammar.title: Blending: reading a word you have never seen
grammar.explanation: You will meet unfamiliar words for the rest of your life. Blending is how you read them without asking anybody: say each sound, then run them together faster until they become the word.
grammar.rule:
s — t — o — p    →  stop
b — u — s        →  bus
f — o — r — m    →  form
n — e — x — t    →  next

Sounds first. Then join. Then say it whole.
grammar.workedExample:
Take d — e — s — k.
1. Say each sound separately: d … e … s … k.
2. Say them again, a little faster: de … sk.
3. Faster again, with no gaps: desk.
4. Now say the whole word once: desk.
The joining is the part that turns sounds into reading. If you stop after step 1, you have four sounds and no word.
grammar.mistake: Many learners say the sounds correctly and then stop, waiting for the word to appear. It will not. Speed is what joins them — say them fast enough to run together and the word arrives on its own.
grammar.tip: Say the sounds faster and faster until they collide. That collision is the word.
grammar.practice:
Blend each one, then say the whole word. None of these are taught in this unit.
1. l — a — m — p
2. m — i — l — k
3. b — e — l — t
4. s — t — a — m — p
5. f — r — o — n — t
grammar.answers: 1. lamp  2. milk  3. belt  4. stamp  5. front. You just read five words nobody taught you. That is what blending is for.

speaking.title: Speaking 1 — The six th words
speaking.instructions:
Use a mirror. You must be able to see your tongue on every one.
Say: the, this, that, they, mother.
Then: three, thank, month, both, thirty-three.
Record all ten. Play it back and mark any that sounded like t, d or s.
Record thirty-three three more times — it is the hardest in the unit.
speaking.tutor: Say thirty-three to the tutor three times and ask whether it heard th or t.

speaking.title: Speaking 2 — Very, ferry, berry, wary
speaking.instructions:
Put a finger on your throat.
Say: very, vest, vine. Your throat should buzz on the first sound.
Say: ferry, form, five. No buzz.
Say: west, work, wary. Round your lips — check in a mirror.
Say: berry, best, bus. Both lips closed first.
Record all twelve in one take. Play it back and mark any two that sounded the same.
speaking.tutor: Ask the tutor to say four of these words and write down which you heard. Then check.

speaking.title: Speaking 3 — Right and light
speaking.instructions:
Decide by feel, not by sound. Your tongue either touches behind your teeth or it does not.
Say: light, led, late, learn, letter. Tongue touches.
Say: right, red, rate, read, ready. Tongue pulls back, touches nothing.
Record all ten. Play it back and mark any pair you cannot tell apart.
If you cannot hear the difference, that is normal — trust the touch instead.
speaking.tutor: Say five of these to the tutor and ask which it heard. Compare with what you meant.

speaking.title: Speaking 4 — Nothing before the s
speaking.instructions:
Build each word up before you say it whole.
s … sc … school
s … st … str … street
s … st … stop
s … sm … small
Then say all four quickly, one after the other.
Record it. Play it back. You are listening for one thing only: a small sound before the s. Mark YES or NO for each word.
speaking.tutor: Say the four words to the tutor and ask whether it heard a vowel before the s.

speaking.title: Speaking 5 — Say only one
speaking.instructions:
Record yourself saying ONE word from each pair, in any order, and do not write down which.
sit / seat · live / leave · full / fool · it / eat · ship / sheep
Wait ten minutes. Then play the recording back and write down what you hear.
Compare with the words you meant to say.
If you have someone with you, do it with them instead — say one word and let them guess.
speaking.tutor: Ask the tutor to say one word from each pair and tell it which you heard.

speaking.title: Speaking 6 — Read it aloud, unprepared
speaking.instructions:
Open Reading 1 — Six Things, and Not All Six Are Yours.
Read the whole text aloud without practising it first.
Record it.
Listen back once and write down the three places you would do differently.
Then record it a second time and keep that one.
speaking.tutor: Read the text to the tutor and ask which of the six sounds still needs work.

writing.title: Writing 1 — Fill in the form
writing.prompt:
Fill in the registration form from Reading 3.
Write in capital letters, as the form asks.
Do not leave any line empty — if a question does not apply to you, write NONE.
You may invent any details you do not want to write down.
Read the last line before you finish.
writing.model:
FAMILY NAME: OSMAN
FIRST NAME: HANA
DATE OF BIRTH: 14 / 03 / 1992
STREET: 12 PARK ROAD
TOWN: NORTHFIELD
PHONE: 070 4456 789
HAVE YOU STUDIED ENGLISH BEFORE? NO
WHICH DAYS: MONDAY, WEDNESDAY, FRIDAY
MORNING OR EVENING: EVENING
PLACE FOR A CHILD? YES
SIGNATURE: H. OSMAN   DATE: 02 / 09 / 2026
writing.criteria: Every line has something written on it; every letter is a capital; the date is in the order the form asks; you noticed the line about bringing a document
writing.support: Do not start at the top. Start with the three easiest lines — name, town, phone — then go back and fill the rest. A form is easier when it is half full.
writing.extension: Write one sentence underneath saying which document you would bring, and why that one.

writing.title: Writing 2 — Six sentences, six sounds
writing.prompt:
Write six sentences about your week.
Each sentence must contain one of this unit's six sounds:
1. a th word   2. a v, f, w or b word   3. an r or l word
4. a word with two consonants together   5. a long vowel   6. a short vowel
Underline the word you chose in each sentence.
writing.model:
1. I have three days free this week.
2. I go to work at seven.
3. Turn left at the corner.
4. My daughter goes to school in this street.
5. I leave the house early.
6. I sit near the window on the bus.
writing.criteria: Six sentences; each carries its assigned sound; the target word underlined; each sentence starts with a capital and ends with a full stop
writing.support: Take the words straight from this unit's six groups. You are practising the sound, not inventing new vocabulary.
writing.extension: Read all six aloud and record them. Listen for the sound you underlined in each one.

writing.title: Writing 3 — Write what you hear
writing.prompt:
Record yourself reading ten words from this unit, in a mixed order. Do not write the list down.
Wait until the next day.
Play the recording back and write what you hear.
Then check against the unit and mark your own work.
Write one sentence saying which sound you got wrong most often.
writing.model:
1. school  2. work  3. month  4. seat  5. right  6. next  7. five  8. this  9. stop  10. live
I got 8 out of 10. Both my mistakes were with r and l — I wrote light for right and collect for correct. I need to check whether my tongue touches.
writing.criteria: Ten words written down; the work marked honestly against the unit; the sentence names a specific sound, not just says it was hard
writing.support: Waiting a day matters — if you play it back straight away you will hear what you meant to say rather than what you said.
writing.extension: Do it again a week later with the same ten words and compare the two scores.

writing.title: Writing 4 — The words you will need this week
writing.prompt:
Look at this unit's six word groups.
Choose the ten words you will actually use in the next seven days.
Write each one, and next to it write where you will use it.
They must be real situations, not examples.
writing.model:
form — at the office on Monday
bus — every morning
school — when I take my daughter
next — asking which stop
right / left — asking the way to the clinic
small — buying a bag
work — telling someone what I do
seat — on the bus when it is full
thank you — every day, many times
month — when someone asks how long I have been here
writing.length: Ten words, each with a real situation
writing.criteria: Ten words from this unit; each paired with a specific real situation; no invented examples
writing.support: Start from your week, not from the word list. Think about Monday first, then find the word that fits it.
writing.extension: Carry the list with you. Tick each word once you have actually said it out loud to someone.

activities.title: Practice 1 — Which of the six are yours?
activities.instructions:
Do this before anything else in the unit. It takes about ten minutes and it decides where you spend the rest of your time.
Record yourself saying these six lines, one after the other:
1. the, this, three, thank, month
2. very, ferry, berry, wary
3. right, light, red, led
4. school, street, stop, small
5. sit, seat, live, leave
6. d — e — s — k … desk
Now play the recording back and answer one question for each line.
1. Can you see your tongue in a mirror when you say them? Yes / No
2. Do all four sound different from each other? Yes / No
3. Do the pairs sound different from each other? Yes / No
4. Is there any sound before the s? Yes / No
5. Is one vowel clearly longer than the other? Yes / No
6. Did the sounds join into a word? Yes / No
Write your six answers down. Keep them.
activities.answers:
There is no right answer — this is about you, not about English.
How to read your six answers: line 1 No, line 2 No, line 3 No, line 4 Yes, line 5 No, line 6 No each mean that area needs work. The opposite answer means it does not.
Most learners find two or three of the six need work, not all six. Whichever ones came back needing work, study those Pattern cards closely and do their Speaking tasks twice. Skim the others once and move on — there is no value in practising a sound you already make correctly.
If you are unsure about any line, treat it as needing work. You will find out quickly.

activities.title: Practice 2 — Voiced or quiet th
activities.instructions:
Put each word in one of two columns: VOICE (your throat buzzes) or QUIET (just air).
Put a finger on your throat to decide.
the · three · this · thank · that · month · they · both · mother · thirty
activities.answers:
VOICE: the, this, that, they, mother. QUIET: three, thank, month, both, thirty.
A pattern worth noticing: the voiced ones are nearly all small grammar words, and the quiet ones are nearly all ordinary vocabulary. That is not a rule, but it will guess right most of the time.

activities.title: Practice 3 — Which of the four?
activities.instructions:
Write F, V, W or B for the sound at the START of each word.
very · form · work · best · five · west · bus · fine · vest · wait
activities.answers:
V: very, vest. F: form, fine, five. W: work, west, wait. B: best, bus.
If you put any word in the wrong column, say it again with a finger on your throat (for V against F) or with a mirror (for W — your lips should make a circle).

activities.title: Practice 4 — Find the extra sound
activities.instructions:
Record yourself saying these five words: school, street, stop, small, next.
Play the recording back.
Write YES or NO next to each: did you add a small sound before or inside the word?
Record again and try to turn every YES into a NO.
If someone is with you, ask them to listen too — it is easier to hear in another person's voice than in your own.
activities.answers:
Your recording is the answer. Almost everybody has at least two YES on the first attempt, and hearing it is most of the fix. If you have none at all, this is one of the six you can skip.
If you cannot hear it even on playback, slow right down and say only the first two sounds of each word: sc, st, st, sm. An added vowel is much more obvious with nothing after it.

activities.title: Practice 5 — Long or short?
activities.instructions:
Record yourself saying ONE word from each pair below, in a mixed order. Do not write down which one you said.
Wait ten minutes, then play it back and write what you hear. Eight pairs:
sit / seat · live / leave · full / fool · it / eat · ship / sheep · fit / feet · pill / peel · chip / cheap
If someone is with you, do it with them instead — say one word and let them write down what they heard.
activities.answers:
Score yourself out of eight by comparing what you wrote with what you meant to say.
Six or more means you are making the difference clearly enough. Below six, exaggerate the long vowel — hold it longer than feels natural — and record again. Too long is still the right word; too short is a different word.

activities.title: Practice 6 — Read a word nobody taught you
activities.instructions:
None of these words appear in this unit. Blend the sounds and read each one aloud.
1. l — a — m — p
2. m — i — l — k
3. b — e — l — t
4. s — t — a — m — p
5. f — r — o — n — t
6. d — r — i — n — k
activities.answers:
1. lamp  2. milk  3. belt  4. stamp  5. front  6. drink.
You read six words that were never taught to you. Notice that numbers 4, 5 and 6 also have two consonants together at the start — blending and clusters are the same skill from two directions.
If any of the six did not arrive, say the sounds faster until they collide. Speed is what joins them.

quizzes.q: Where should your tongue be for the th in three?
options: At the roof of your mouth
At the back of your throat
quizzes.why: Both th sounds need the tongue forward, between the teeth. Behind the teeth gives you t or d, which is the usual substitution.

quizzes.q: Which word uses your voice on the th sound?
quizzes.why: This is voiced — your throat buzzes. Thank, three and month are all the quiet th, made with air only.

quizzes.q: Very and ferry start with different sounds. What is the difference?
options: One uses the voice and one does not
quizzes.a: One uses the voice and one does not
quizzes.why: Both put the top teeth on the bottom lip — the mouth position is identical. Only the voice differs: v buzzes, f does not.

quizzes.q: For which sound does the tip of your tongue touch just behind your top teeth?
quizzes.why: L touches. R pulls back and touches nothing, w uses rounded lips, and v uses teeth on lip.

quizzes.q: A learner says iskool instead of school. What has happened?
options: A vowel was added before the s
The vowel was made too long
quizzes.a: A vowel was added before the s
quizzes.why: Many languages do not allow two consonants at the start of a word, so a vowel gets inserted to make it sayable. Nothing was left out — something was added.

quizzes.q: Which word does NOT begin with two consonants together?
quizzes.why: Office begins with a single vowel sound. The other three all start with a consonant cluster.

quizzes.q: I live here and I leave here mean different things. What makes the difference?
quizzes.why: Live has a short vowel and leave a long one. Everything else in the two words is the same, which is why a listener can quietly understand the wrong one.

quizzes.q: Blend these sounds: b — e — l — t
quizzes.why: The four sounds run together as belt. Bell drops the final sound, and bolt and built each change the vowel you were given.

quizzes.q: Will all six of this unit's sounds be hard for you?
options: No — it depends on the language you already speak
Yes, they are hard for everybody
Only if you learn English as an adult
quizzes.a: No — it depends on the language you already speak
quizzes.why: Every language uses a different set of sounds. A sound your language already has will not trouble you; one it does not have will take work. That is why Practice 1 comes first.

quizzes.q: The registration form says to write in capital letters. Where does it say so?
options: At the bottom, after the signature
At the top, before the boxes
quizzes.a: At the top, before the boxes
quizzes.why: It is the second line of the form. Instructions usually come before the thing they apply to.

quizzes.q: What must you bring with the registration form?
options: One document showing your name and date of birth
quizzes.a: One document showing your name and date of birth
quizzes.why: The final line of the form says so. It is easy to miss because most people stop reading at the signature.

quizzes.q: According to Reading 2, what is the fix when someone does not understand you?
options: Speak a little slower and put the sound in the right place
quizzes.a: Speak a little slower and put the sound in the right place
quizzes.why: The text names speaking louder specifically in order to rule it out — volume was never the problem.

teacherNotes.note: The course is designed for self-access and this unit assumes nobody is present. Practice 1 replaces the diagnostic a teacher would normally do by ear, every grammar card carries a worked example and an answer key, and every speaking task is checked by recording and playback rather than by correction. If you are running it with a group, everything below is an accelerator, not a repair.

It is not an alphabet unit and must not be taught as one. Adult learners arrive literate in some script and mostly decoding Latin letters. Opening with letter recognition is the fastest way to lose an adult class. Start from Practice 1 and let each learner discover their own two or three problem areas.

In a mixed group, no two learners will have the same subset of the six. Do not drill all six with everybody — it wastes the time of learners who already have four of them. Use Practice 1 to sort the group, then run the areas as short parallel stations. The one that most often needs whole-group attention is consonant clusters, because it is the most audible and the hardest to self-detect.

The added vowel in clusters is nearly impossible to feel and easy to hear on playback. Learners who avoid recording themselves make slower progress on this unit than on any other. If you are with a group, do the first playback together so nobody faces their own recording alone the first time.

The AI tutor is a rehearsal partner, not a marking service, and its pronunciation feedback is indicative only. No task in this unit is scored by the tutor alone. Learners must not be asked to give the tutor personal, immigration, medical or financial details; the registration form in Reading 3 is a practice document and may be completed with invented details.

selfAssessment.statement: I know which of the six sounds are hard for me.
I can say the and three with my tongue between my teeth.
I can say very, ferry, berry and wary so they sound like four different words.
I can say school and street without adding a sound at the start.
I can hear whether someone said sit or seat.
I can read a short word I have never seen before.

assignment.title: The six sounds, recorded
assignment.instructions: Record one continuous take, no more than three minutes, in which you: say the ten th words; say very, ferry, berry and wary; say five r words and five l words; say school, street, stop, small and next; say four long-and-short pairs; and finally read Reading 1 aloud from beginning to end. Keep your Practice 1 answers with it, so the recording can be compared against the six areas you identified at the start.
assignment.submissionType: Audio recording and the Practice 1 result
